messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Hairdresser
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Photos): Related photos, Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Nabil is a 38-year-old Middle Eastern American man who has worked for years as a hairdresser, someone used to being on his feet all day, close to other people’s faces and bodies, making conversation while watching himself and his clients in the mirror. His difficulties began after a life-threatening illness that required repeated hospital examinations and procedures. What stays with him most is not a single tidy memory but a series of sensory fragments from that period: the sharp medical smell in procedure rooms, the pain in his body during treatment, the helpless dread of waiting to hear what would happen next. At the time he became intensely aware that his body could fail him without warning, and he has never fully recovered his sense that it is a trustworthy place to live.

In the months afterward, reminders began to break into ordinary life. If he sees photos from that period—pictures of himself looking gaunt, hospital images saved on his phone, even medical-looking images online—his body reacts immediately. He feels a rush of fear and horror, his muscles tighten, and he becomes acutely braced, as if danger is already underway. The same thing happens when he wakes from a nightmare and is left with that lingering half-awake feeling that the illness is still happening, and it becomes especially intense when he has to attend a medical examination. Those moments do not just upset him; they pull him straight back into the bodily emergency of the illness.

The reminders also bring back the trauma in a fragmented, sensory way. Looking at photos or waking with dream residue can be enough for him to catch the same hospital odor in his mind, vivid enough that he sometimes pauses and scans the room as if it might actually be there. During or after a medical appointment, he may feel pain in the same part of his body that hurt during the illness, even when the current procedure is routine. Sometimes there is no clear picture at all—just the full force of terror and helplessness dropping onto him without an image, as though the feeling arrives before any memory can organize it. When that happens, the emotional wave itself convinces him that the past is not really past.

What has made these episodes more frightening is the meaning Nabil has come to give them. He says his body behaves like an enemy, launching into alarm even when he knows intellectually that he is safe. He has become convinced that he can no longer trust his own body, and in his worst moments he worries that reactions this strong mean he is going crazy. Those beliefs intensify his fear: once he notices his heart racing, tension building, or a surge of shame and panic, he no longer experiences it as a passing stress response but as proof that something inside him is fundamentally wrong and uncontrollable. The more he interprets his reactions this way, the more persistently on edge he feels.

Those appraisals also shape how he experiences the memories themselves. Because he is so frightened by his own reactions, even a flicker of remembered pain or a trace of the medical smell becomes loaded with extra meaning. He listens inwardly for signs that his body is about to betray him again, and this seems to make the sensory fragments more available, more invasive. He has become highly watchful for anything that could set him off. At work in the salon, where mirrors surround him all day, he notices photographs more quickly than other people do and has become uneasy when clients show phone pictures of themselves from periods of illness or recovery. If he has had a nightmare the night before, he arrives already tense, scanning himself and the room, making him more likely to latch onto some reminder and react.

Once the memories are stirred, they feed the sense of current threat. A phantom trace of the hospital smell or a burst of recalled pain makes his whole body lock up; he feels physically reactive, tense, and ready for catastrophe. On those days he trims appointments short, steps into the back room to compose himself, or becomes less talkative with clients because he is trying to hide how frightened he feels. The emotional intensity without a clear image is especially destabilizing because he cannot explain it to himself; he only knows that his body seems to be reliving something he cannot fully control. That in turn makes him even more sensitive to waking from nightmares, seeing photos, or facing medical procedures, because he has come to expect that any of these could unravel him.

By the time he sought help, the pattern had tightened. He had delayed routine follow-up care because medical appointments felt unbearable, and he was increasingly preoccupied by what it meant that his body still reacted this way. What finally brought him in was a recent morning after a nightmare when he went to work already shaken, smelled the salon chemicals through the haze of sleep, and for a moment was certain he was back in treatment and losing his mind. More than anything, Nabil is afraid that his body will never feel like his own again. What he hopes for, cautiously, is to be able to walk into a medical office—or simply wake from sleep—without feeling that he is stepping back into mortal danger.
